title: Quantifiers, Scope and Translation
quickIdea: Propositional logic cannot say 'all' or 'some'. Quantifiers add that, and the rules for negating and reordering them are what GATE tests alongside propositional tautologies.
remember: Universal quantifier: for all x, P(x). Existential: there exists x with P(x). Both range over a stated domain.
Negation: not (for all x P(x)) = there exists x with not P(x); not (there exists x P(x)) = for all x not P(x).
Quantifier order matters: for all x there exists y R(x,y) does not imply there exists y such that for all x R(x,y).

Restricted domains are written with implication for universal and conjunction for existential: 'all students pass' is for all x (student(x) -> pass(x)); 'some student passes' is there exists x (student(x) and pass(x)).
A variable is bound inside the scope of its quantifier and free outside it; a formula with free variables has no truth value until they are assigned.
A closed formula is a tautology when it is true in every domain and every interpretation of its predicates.

example.prompt: Negate: for all x (P(x) -> there exists y Q(x,y)).
example.work: The outer negation turns for all into there exists and negates the body; then not (A -> B) = A and not B, and the inner negation turns there exists into for all.
example.answer: there exists x (P(x) and for all y not Q(x,y))

gateAngle: GATE 2015 Set 2 Q.55 asks which first-order formula is a tautology. The answer is the one whose two sides differ only by rewriting P(x,y) -> R(x,y) as not P(x,y) or R(x,y), giving the propositional shape A <-> A. Spot the propositional skeleton first.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Over the integers, which of these hold: for all x there exists y (x < y), or there exists y for all x (x < y)?
variations.answer: The first holds; the second does not
variations.why: For any integer x, y = x + 1 is larger, so the first is true. No single integer exceeds all integers, so the second fails. Swapping quantifiers of different kinds changes meaning.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Translate 'every student likes some teacher' and 'some teacher is liked by every student' into quantifiers over students S and teachers T.
variations.answer: for all s there exists t L(s,t); versus there exists t for all s L(s,t)
variations.why: The two differ only in quantifier order, and the second is strictly stronger: one teacher must serve every student.

trap.what: Using AND with a universal quantifier, or OR with an existential one, when translating from English.
trap.why: 'All students pass' is not for all x (student(x) and pass(x)) - that claims everything in the domain is a passing student. The universal needs implication, the existential needs conjunction.
trap.counterexample: Domain {a teacher}, nobody is a student. for all x (student(x) -> pass(x)) is vacuously true, while for all x (student(x) and pass(x)) is false.

check.question: Negate: there exists x (P(x) and Q(x)).
check.answer: for all x (not P(x) or not Q(x))
check.explanation: The quantifier flips and the body is negated; De Morgan turns the conjunction into a disjunction of negations.
